issues.legal_issue: A power to annul transfers designed to defeat an estate-acquisition law is protected from challenge under fundamental-rights guarantees when it is an integral, ancillary part of that law.
material_facts: The estate in which the disputed plots were situated vested in the State under the land reform law.
The Collector found that the claimed settlement was a paper transaction made to defeat the law and annulled it.
The annulment power was intended to prevent anticipatory transfers and to make the estate-acquisition law effective.
issues.conclusion: The annulment power was protected by Article 31A and could not be invalidated on the grounds that it infringed Articles 14, 19 or 31.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(a) protects laws providing for State acquisition of an estate or rights in it, or extinguishment or modification of those rights, from challenges under Articles 14, 19 and 31. A provision that is ancillary to and integral with such a law is assessed in the setting of the law as a whole, rather than in isolation. The Court applied Thakur Raghubir Singh v. State of Ajmer, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 478.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A party challenges the validity of a power forming part of a law directed to land reform.
predicates.measure_acquires_estate_rights: The law provides for the State to acquire an estate or rights in an estate.
predicates.measure_extinguishes_estate_rights: The law provides for rights in an estate to be extinguished or modified.
predicates.annulment_power_is_integral_to_measure: The annulment power is an ancillary part of the law, intended to prevent transfers that would defeat its estate-reform purpose.

issues.definition: When a land-reform measure acquires or alters estate rights and an annulment power is integral to that measure, the power is protected from the stated fundamental-rights challenge.

issues.legal_issue: A retrospective amendment expressly deeming changes to the Collector’s transfer-review power always effective governs the Collector’s authority in a pending challenge to that authority.
material_facts: The High Court set aside the Collector’s order on the ground that the Collector lacked authority to determine whether the settlement had been made after the relevant statutory threshold.
The amending law expressly provided that specified changes to the Collector’s power were to be deemed always to have been made.
The State relied on those changes in its appeal, and the Court held that the amended law clearly conferred the disputed authority.
issues.conclusion: The specified changes to the Collector’s authority operated retrospectively, and the High Court’s ruling that the Collector lacked that authority could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed section 3(iv)(a) and (b) of the Bihar Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1959, according to their express language deeming the relevant omissions and insertions always effective. It held that the amended section clearly empowered the Collector to determine whether a transfer had been made after the statutory threshold.

predicates.appeal_from_ruling_on_collectors_authori: An appeal challenges a ruling that a Collector lacked authority to decide whether a transfer fell within the Collector’s statutory review power.
predicates.amendment_expressly_deems_power_change_a: An amendment expressly states that a change to the Collector’s power is deemed always to have been in effect.

issues.definition: In an appeal concerning the Collector’s authority, an amendment that expressly deems the power change always effective makes that change retrospective.

issues.legal_issue: A requirement of subsequent State confirmation does not apply to a Collector’s annulment order made under the prior version of the law when the required prior State sanction was obtained.
material_facts: The Collector made the annulment order before the amending law came into force.
Under the prior version of the law, the Collector obtained the State Government’s previous sanction before making the order.
The amendment removed the previous-sanction wording and added a proviso requiring confirmation before an order could take effect or possession be taken.
issues.conclusion: For an order made before the amendment came into force, the previous sanction obtained under the prior law was sufficient; subsequent confirmation was not required.
issues.legal_principle: On its construction of section 3(iv)(c) and section 3(v) of the Bihar Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1959, the Court held that the removal of the previous-sanction requirement was prospective, while the confirmation proviso was also prospective. Requiring later confirmation of a pre-amendment order would conflict with the amendment’s treatment of previous sanction and produce redundant or incongruous requirements.

predicates.collector_annulment_order: The Collector made an order annulling a transfer.
predicates.order_under_prior_version: The Collector made the order under the version of the law that applied before the amendment.
predicates.prior_state_sanction_obtained: The State Government gave its sanction before the Collector made the order.

issues.definition: When the Collector made an annulment order under the prior version of the law after obtaining prior State sanction, that sanction suffices without later confirmation.

issues.legal_issue: A Collector’s annulment order made under the amended law requires State Government confirmation before it takes effect or possession is taken under it.
material_facts: The amendment added a proviso stating that an annulment order would not take effect and possession would not be taken unless the State Government confirmed the order.
The Court held that the new confirmation requirement applied prospectively to orders made after the amendment came into force.
issues.conclusion: For an annulment order made after the amendment came into force, subsequent confirmation by the State Government is required before the order takes effect or possession is taken.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(v) of the Bihar Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1959, added a confirmation proviso that the Court construed as prospective. The Court distinguished this requirement from the previous-sanction requirement applicable to orders under the prior version of the law.

predicates.collector_annulment_order: The Collector made an order annulling a transfer.
predicates.order_under_amended_version: The Collector made the order under the version of the law that applied after the amendment.

issues.definition: When the Collector makes an annulment order under the amended version of the law, State confirmation is required before the order takes effect or possession is taken.

issues.legal_issue: A procedural objection to a Collector’s order will not be considered for the first time on appeal when it was not specifically alleged below or raised in argument below.
material_facts: The respondent’s supporting affidavit in the High Court did not specifically allege that the Collector had failed to conduct the required inquiry or obtain the required prior sanction.
The parties did not raise those matters in argument before the High Court.
The respondent sought to raise the matters for the first time in the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to consider the procedural objections because they were raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that, in the circumstances, it was not justified in allowing a party to raise for the first time on appeal an objection that had not been specifically alleged in the supporting affidavit or raised in argument before the lower court.

predicates.appeal_to_supreme_court: A party seeks to raise an objection in an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.procedural_objection_not_specifically_pl: The party did not specifically allege the procedural objection in the material filed before the lower court.
predicates.procedural_objection_not_raised_in_lower: The party did not raise the objection in argument before the lower court.

issues.definition: In a Supreme Court appeal, a procedural objection not specifically pleaded or argued below is not entertained when raised for the first time on appeal.
